profile.regional_context: QTS was founded in 2003 by Chad Williams, went public via IPO in 2013, and was acquired by Blackstone (via Blackstone Infrastructure Partners and BREIT) for approximately $10 billion, completed August 31, 2021. QTS is headquartered in Overland Park, Kansas.
profile.facility_type_note: Part of QTS's Northern Virginia campus, spanning Loudoun County (Ashburn-Shellhorn, Ashburn-Moran, Ashburn Lockridge buildings), Prince William County (Manassas DC1, DC2, DC5), and Sterling (Ashburn 1, Ashburn 2). Northern Virginia is confirmed by Wikipedia as one of QTS's primary operating regions, alongside the separate Richmond, VA campus recorded elsewhere in this registry.

reading.body:
QTS Ashburn 1 publishes 55 MW of IT capacity across two Sterling, Virginia facilities, ranking it fifth among the nineteen Virginia data centers in this dataset that disclose a megawatt figure.

The 55 MW figure translates to roughly 1,375 racks at 40 kW per rack, the density typical of AI training workloads, or 5,500 racks at 10 kW per rack for colocation. A second building listed as under construction means the published capacity may not reflect the completed campus. The operator, Quality Technology Services, has not disclosed final specifications for the combined site.

LEED certification addresses building energy and environmental design but does not certify uptime tier, security posture, or federal compliance. No Uptime Institute tier rating, SOC attestation, or federal security designation appears on the operator's published spec page. The facility's resilience and compliance profile therefore remains undisclosed.

Virginia holds 326 mapped facilities in this dataset, but only nineteen publish a megawatt figure. Those nineteen sum to 1,326 MW. At 55 MW, this campus represents roughly 4 percent of Virginia's published total. Most Virginia facilities publish no capacity figure at all, so the state's true installed IT capacity is larger by an unknown margin. The Ashburn corridor's concentration in Virginia's disclosed figures reflects that publicly available data skews toward larger, more transparent operators.
